learn.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
learn.html:
Countable nouns can be counted (one apple, two apples). Uncountable nouns are not counted one by one: they are substances or masses (rice, milk, bread).

CountableUncountable
Examplesegg, banana, potato, cookierice, milk, bread, cheese, pasta, meat
a / ana banana, an eggNo: a rice (incorrect)
Pluralbananas, eggs, potatoesThey have no plural
VerbThe eggs are fresh.The milk is fresh.
  • Special plurals: tomato → tomatoes, potato → potatoes, strawberry → strawberries.
  • To count an uncountable noun, use a measure: a glass of milk, a piece of bread, two bags of rice.
  • Meat, bread, cheese, fish, pasta and fruit are usually uncountable in English.

watch.why: Uncountable nouns take a singular verb.

watch.wrong: She eats a lot of potatos.
watch.right: She eats a lot of potatoes.
I need two pieces of bread.
watch.why: To count an uncountable noun, use a measure.

learn.title: How much / How many / a lot of
learn.html:
To ask about and talk about quantities.

Used withQuestionNegativeAffirmative
UncountableHow much milk do we need?We don't need much milk.We need a lot of milk.
Countable (plural)How many eggs do we need?We don't need many eggs.We need a lot of eggs.
  • much and many are mostly used in questions and negatives.
  • In affirmative sentences a lot of is more natural (it works for both types of noun).
  • Possible answers: A lot. / Not much. / Not many. / Two bottles.
  • How much also asks about price: How much is the soup?

watch.why: In affirmative sentences, don't use much/many: use a lot of.

learn.title: some / any
learn.html:
They are used with plurals and with uncountable nouns when the exact amount doesn't matter.

TypeWordExample
AffirmativesomeWe have some cheese and some tomatoes.
Negativenot anyWe don't have any bread.
QuestionanyDo you have any eggs?
Offer or requestsomeWould you like some coffee? Can I have some water?
  • With singular countable nouns use a / an: I'd like a sandwich.
  • No + noun means not any: There's no milk. = There isn't any milk.

watch.why: Don't use two negatives: isn't any.

learn.title: would like: offering and asking
learn.html:
Would like is a polite way of saying I want. It is the same for all persons, and it is used a lot for offering and asking.

UseStructureExample
OfferWould you like + noun?Would you like some tea?
Offer with a verbWould you like + to + verb?Would you like to go out for dinner?
RequestI'd like + nounI'd like a salad, please.
Open questionWhat would you like?What would you like to drink?
  • Answers: Yes, please. / No, thanks. / I'd like some water, please.
  • I'd = I would. Don't use do/does with would.
  • After would like + verb, always use to: I'd like to try Thai food.

watch.wrong: I would like have a soda.
watch.right: I would like a soda. / I would like to have a soda.
watch.why: Would like + noun, or would like + to + verb.

watch.wrong: Do you would like some water?
watch.why: Would doesn't use do: invert would + subject.

watch.wrong: I want a coffee, please. (at a restaurant)
watch.why: I'd like sounds more polite than I want.
Would like doesn't change with she.

learn.title: Expressions for ordering food
learn.html:
• A table for two, please. — asking for a table.
  • Can we see the menu? / Are you ready to order? — asking for the menu; the waiter asks if you are ready to order.
  • I'd like the soup, please. / I'll have the chicken. — ordering a dish.
  • Would you like anything to drink? — Some water, please. — offering and accepting.
  • No, thanks. / Yes, please. — refusing or accepting politely.
  • Is everything OK? — Yes, it's delicious. — the waiter asks about the food.
  • Can we have the bill, please? — asking for the bill.
  • … or something? / … or anything? — open list: Do you want a sandwich or something? I don't eat fish or anything like that.

reading.title: Dinner at La Cocina de Lupe
reading.intro: Read the restaurant review and answer.
paragraphs: Last Saturday, my family and I went to La Cocina de Lupe, a small restaurant near my house. We didn't make a reservation, but there was a free table. It was a busy night and there were a lot of people. The restaurant is not very big, but it is warm and friendly.

The waiter brought the menu and asked, "Would you like something to drink?" My father wanted a glass of water, my mother ordered a cup of coffee, and the children asked for some orange juice. For the starter, we ordered a big bowl of soup and some bread. There wasn't much butter on the table, so we asked for some more.

For the main course, I had grilled chicken with rice and vegetables. My sister doesn't eat meat, so she had pasta with tomatoes and cheese. She didn't want any salad. The portions were very big, so we didn't eat all the food.

For dessert, we shared a piece of chocolate cake and some ice cream. The waiter asked, "Would you like anything else?" We said, "Just the bill, please." The bill wasn't expensive, and we left a ten percent tip. I recommend this restaurant. The food is delicious and the service is fast. Next time, I'd like to try the fish tacos!

to divide something with others (we shared)
